messages.subject: Slidify: Reproducible HTML5 Slides Made Easy!
messages.subject_clean: Slidify: Reproducible HTML5 Slides Made Easy!
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Given the flurry of interest in generating reproducible HTML5 slides using knitR, I have taken a quick crack at writing an R package that simplifies the process significantly. It is available on github at http://ramnathv.github.com/slidify and you can see the slides I generated at http://ramnathv.github.com/slidify/slides.html.

The basic idea is to

1. Write your slides in R Markdown
2. Separate slides using ---
3. Run slidify('slides.Rmd')

and you are done!!

I have kept it modular, so that you can write an Rmd document once, and render it using deck.js, html5slides, dzslides, shower, slidy etc. Syntax highlighting can be done either using highlight.js or the highlight package in R and you can style your source code using any of the available themes provided. You can also add custom css and javascript to the default folders and slidify will automatically include it in the html output.

Slidify is still version 0.0.1 and I am still in the process of writing detailed documentation. For most of you in this group, I presume looking through the source code should work well !

Please use the github repository if you have issues while trying to use slidify.

Best,
Ramnath

messages.subject: a verb for making silk?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Yesterday I added a new function silk() to knitr, which can be used to
translate R scripts to Rnw, Rmd and Rhtml, etc. For example:

source: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/inst/examples/knitr-silk.R
output: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/inst/examples/knitr-silk.Rmd

I'm wondering if there is a better verb in English for this task
(first make silk, then knit). The current name silk() came from "make
a silk purse out of a sow's ear", and the idea was contributed by
Richard FitzJohn (https://github.com/richfitz/sowsear).

I looked up the dictionary; silking seems to be often related to corn. Thanks!

Regards,
Yihui

messages.body_plain:
Chunks without labels are assigned labels of the form unnamed-chunk-i
(http://yihui.name/knitr/options), e.g.

library(knitr)
knit(text = '<<>>=
1+1
@
')

  |>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>                                 |  50%
label: unnamed-chunk-1

messages.body_plain:
setwd() is bad, dirty, ugly... you should never use it inside your Rnw
document; use this convention: data files go with source files, and
always start R in the directory of the source files. Whenever you want
to manipulate files, they are assumed to be under the same directory
of your source (e.g. Rnw documents). Then you can always use relative
paths and you will never need to setwd(). Using setwd() contradicts
with the principle of reproducibility, e.g. you use setwd('foo/bar/')
and the directory may not exist in other people's computers. See FAQ
7: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/FAQ.md

1. RStudio always use the directory of the Rnw file as the working directory;
2. opts_chunk is supposed to set chunk options, and working directory
is NOT a chunk option;
3. dependson is completely irrelevant here; have you read the
documentation? http://yihui.name/knitr/options

messages.body_plain:
To chime in here, I completely understand and have bought into the
thou-shalt-not-setwd(). But I have recently run into a situation where
I really wish there was some way to get knitr documents from elsewhere
within a directory structure. Here's the use case that really got me:

Working on my dissertation proposal I have a huge document with many
sub .rnws (that's fine, I just used \include{} in one master tex file
so each section was segregated enough). For each section I generally
have one r script that imports data, cleans it up, fits models (let's
call this setup.r), and then a bunch of individual r scripts for each
plot. When I went to make slides for my defense I wanted to use the
setup.r for each section in place so I didn't have to copy it along
with all of the data into the slides folder, just to use it in the
slides. Allowing for something like this would of course make the
slides a little bit harder to reproduce (they would depend on a
directory structure elsewhere), but it makes the entire project more
coherent (and possible reproducible as well?): the data and processing
scripts are all in a singel place, no need to diff each to see if
there are any differences between them. Additionally if the data is
nontrivially large, having multiple copies of it laying around could
be problematic.

I've run into something similar a few other times, and will admit this
particular use case might actually be an edge case. I'm not sure
there's a way to implement something like this without making it very
tempting for others to set paths like
/root/directories/that/will/be/deleted/foo.R

-Jon

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] disappearance of 'parser'?
messages.body_plain:
I think we could certainly get parser patched to pass check, but I do not think this is a good solution.  Perhaps that's a minority opinion.

First, I doubt CRAN will accept parser without having a single individual committed to be the maintainer.  Down the road this package would become an Achilles heel of anyone depending on it.

IMHO, it's not clear that parser package is the most sensible way to accomplish knitr objectives.   Philosophically it seems strange that knitr should handle the syntax highlighting at all, since all other formatting is handled by the output language (html or latex), both of which have syntax highlighting.  At best this sounds like a recommended package rather than a core dependency as far as knitr is concerned?

If the goal is to at least tag R function names as functions so they can be highlighted, there's probably a more robust way to do this, working either with the base parser or by working with one of the standard syntax highlighter approaches?

What other packages are broken by parser? formatR, which provides tidy, right?  perhaps this is more challenging to address?

In short, I'm not sure that there is an easy fix, in the long run building what we need from the ground up or on well-established dependencies will probably pay off better than patching parser.  Hate to be a downer on this one, happy to be convinced otherwise.

-Carl

After all the efforts that went into the highlight and parser
packages, it would be a shame to dismiss them too quickly because of a
technical glitch and unreliable communication. As far as I'm concerned
they do provide the best solution to the highlighting problem, and
have been a great step forward in this area (compare with regular
Sweave, and/or listings).

Do we know for sure that Romain has decidedly moved away from R? Could
it be that he's been busy with other things for a few months, and that
a temporary fix is all that's needed? I think we ought to contact him,
somehow (old-fashioned phone?).
And regarding that, highlight + parser rely on Rcpp: any luck on that
side, contacting Dirk E. who probably has some useful clues?

Just my 2 cents.

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Thank you all for the suggestions and help. I guess parser and
highlight are not coming back very soon, and Prof Riley required me to
do something before June 25 to avoid being orphaned. Given the tight
time constraint, I have come up with a very naive syntax highlighter
which gives you similar appearance but does not depend on
parser/highlight any more. Also this will not affect R markdown users,
since syntax highlighting is done by a JS library there. It seems many
users are happy with markdown, so the impact of this change will not
be significant. LaTeX users can always use sophisticated syntax
highlighting packages like listings and minted, etc, which do not
depend on R packages. HTML users can always use JS libraries. If you
know how to install highlight/parser from the archived source, knitr
will make use of these packages just like before.

I'll put up the changes to github later. Then we can discuss whether
we should improve my naive syntax highlighter, or save
parser/highlight.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: disappearance of 'parser'?
messages.body_plain:
Below is what ESS does for replacing = with <-. Replacement based on
regular expressions will never be accurate; parser is based on lexical
analysis, so it can find out the equal's which precisely mean
assignments.

(defun ess-fix-EQ-assign (&optional dont-query verbose not-all)
  "Replace \"=\" by \"<-\" in places where it 'might make sense', e.g.,
for function assignments and lines not ending in \",\".
Be *careful* for list()s of functions and when argument not-all is
nil (as by default) !"
  ;;TODO: "in the few places we can be very sure.."
  ;;---- is hard in general: local functions: ok; but functions in
  ;;  list(a = function(x) abs(x), b= function(y) bound(y))  *NOT* ok!
  (interactive "P")
  (ess-replace-regexp-dump-to-src
   "^\\( *[a-z.][_a-z.0-9]*\\) *= *\\(function *(\\)"
   "\\1 <- \\2" dont-query verbose)

  (unless not-all
    ;; "too" aggressive {proposing to replace function argument specs}:
    (ess-replace-regexp-dump-to-src ;; all those *not* ending in ","
     ;; including  Mat[ i, ] = ...,
     ;; but not `names(x) = "..."' for that is "confused" with plot(x=x,..)
     "^\\( *[a-z.][][, \"_a-z.0-9]*\\) *= *\\([a-z.0-9({]\\(.*[^,]\\)? *$\\)"
     "\\1 <- \\2" nil ;; always query - often has many "false positives"
     verbose)
    ))
